text.en: A small magnet sticks to a fridge door, but not to a wooden table. Why? Magnets seem magical, but they follow clear rules that we can test.

A magnet attracts some materials, such as iron, nickel and cobalt. These are magnetic materials. Materials like wood, plastic, glass, paper and rubber are not attracted. They are non-magnetic. Test by bringing a magnet near an object and seeing if it sticks.
In a bar magnet, the pull is usually strongest near the two ends, called the poles. They are the north pole and the south pole. If we break a magnet, each piece still has two poles. A freely hanging bar magnet comes to rest pointing north and south.
Unlike poles attract each other. A north pole pulls a south pole. Like poles repel each other. Two north poles push apart. In these classroom tests, repulsion by a known magnet is a sure sign of another magnet. Attraction alone proves less, because an ordinary piece of iron is attracted too.
A magnetic compass has a small magnetised needle that points north and south. We use a compass to find directions when we are lost or at sea.
Magnets are used in fridge doors, speakers, toys, cranes and in separating iron from waste. Keep strong magnets away from magnetic-stripe cards and sensitive devices. Follow your teacher’s safety rules and the device instructions.

Use a large classroom bar magnet with your teacher. Keep magnets out of your mouth and leave tiny loose magnets alone. Choose a wooden ruler, a plastic cap, aluminium foil and a steel paper clip to test.
Make a prediction for each object. Put them on a plain wooden or plastic table and bring the same end of the magnet near each one, starting about the same distance away.

board.text: Keep the magnet and starting gap alike

text.en: Watch for the object to move before it touches the magnet. The steel paper clip usually moves toward it, while ordinary aluminium foil does not noticeably move toward a classroom magnet.
The foil and the paper clip are both made of metal, but they react differently. A material can look shiny and still belong in the non-magnetic group in our test.

board.text: Metal appearance cannot tell us the result

text.en: Place a sheet of paper over the steel clip and hold the magnet just above the paper. You may still see the clip move. The magnet can act across a small gap, so it does not have to touch the clip.

board.text: Magnet → paper and small gap → clip

text.en: Test the pull near one end of a bar magnet and then near its middle with the same steel clip. Begin at the same distance each time. Compare how readily the clip moves.

board.text: Change the spot on the bar magnet

text.en: The pull is usually much easier to notice near either end. The two poles are the two end regions of this bar magnet. A weaker pull in the middle does not mean there is no effect there.

board.text: Bar magnet: stronger pull near either end

text.en: Imagine a drawing of a bar magnet divided into two pieces. Draw an N and an S on each piece to show what would happen. This is a picture exercise, so leave the real magnet whole.

board.text: Draw N and S on each imagined piece

text.en: Watch a bar magnet that your teacher hangs freely from a thread, away from iron objects and other magnets. Let it settle, then note where each end points.
Turn the hanging magnet a little and release it. It may swing for a while, but after it settles its north-seeking end should point about the same way again.
Set a compass flat on a wooden table and let the needle settle. The north-seeking end of the needle gives an approximate direction for north. The opposite end shows south.
Iron nearby or a second magnet can affect the compass. If the needle gives an unexpected direction on a steel shelf, try moving to a table away from metal furniture and let it settle again.

board.text: Check for steel and nearby magnets

text.en: With two marked classroom bar magnets, hold one steady and let the other slide on the table. Predict what the movable magnet will do when the two north ends approach.
If the north ends stay facing each other, the movable magnet tends to slide away. Turn it so its south end faces the north end, and it tends to slide toward the other magnet.
An unmarked object that is pulled toward a magnet could be an ordinary piece of iron. If it pushes away from a known pole in the same kind of test, that is evidence the object is itself a magnet.
Imagine a dry tray with sand and steel clips mixed together. Predict what happens when you pass a classroom magnet in a thin paper sleeve close above the mixture.

board.text: Separate sand and steel with a magnet

text.en: The clips are attracted to the magnet through the sleeve, while most of the sand stays in the tray. Move the magnet away from the sleeve over a second tray and the clips fall off.

board.text: Sand remains in the original tray

problem.en: How can you find which end of an unmarked bar magnet is north?

text.en: Hang it from a thread so it turns freely.
The end that points north is the north pole.

why.en: The Earth acts like a giant magnet.

prompt.en: A friend says a magnet attracts everything. How would you show it does not?

requiredIdeas.en: The iron is attracted in this set of tests, while the wood and plastic are not.

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking all metals are magnetic or that all types of steel behave the same way.

points.en: Magnets attract iron, nickel and cobalt.
Like poles repel and unlike attract.
